source.title: Efficient Global Optimization of Two-layer ReLU Networks: Quadratic-time Algorithms and Adversarial Training
source.authors: Yatong Bai; Tanmay Gautam; S. Sojoudi

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some equations and symbols are garbled by text extraction, but the relevant experimental results and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares gradient-based back-propagation training with convex training and reports training losses on CIFAR-10, providing a different-method test of whether the reported gradient recipe reaches low training error. Its experiments concern binary classification with a one-hidden-layer ReLU network, not the broader deep-network conditions in the claim.
record.gate_note: The CIFAR-10 comparison in Table 5 and the downsampled CIFAR-10 comparison in Table 3 report training loss for back-propagation gradient descent and convex training. The paper also reports validation accuracies and adversarial accuracies, which do not independently measure the claim's training-error outcome. Other CIFAR-10 accuracy results are not separate rows because they do not report training classification error.
record.test_reason: The study compares convex optimization with back-propagation for one-hidden-layer fully connected ReLU networks. Its training losses and regularized objectives do not measure V1's training classification error in large convolutional networks. It does not test teacher-student local-minimum frequencies, depth degradation, initialization-dependent trainability, stability thresholds, or batch-normalization speedups.
record.authors_conclusion: The record correctly summarizes the lower standard-training loss and absence of reported gradient-model training classification error. Its convergence summary needs qualification: exact convex training has global convergence guarantees under stated assumptions; sampled formulations target approximate solutions, and convex adversarial training optimizes an upper bound on the non-convex adversarial optimum.
record.recipe_differences: The comparisons use one-hidden-layer ReLU networks and squared or hinge loss; the principal CIFAR-10 comparison is on a 600-image, downsampled binary subset, not the claim's large convolutional networks or CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification-error measure.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and task scope differ across the CIFAR-10 results: downsampled birds-versus-ships binary subset; squared-loss and hinge-loss experiments; standard and adversarial training recipes.

fits_no_version.finding: On downsampled binary CIFAR-10, ADMM achieves a lower regularized squared training loss than back-propagation within comparable time: 607.6 versus 991.5.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Convex training can reduce the regularized training objective faster than back-propagation in some one-hidden-layer fully connected networks.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 5 reports standard-training objectives of .3146 for GD-std and .006910 for Algorithm 2.1; adversarial objectives are .8370 for GD-FGSM, .8220 for GD-PGD and .6511 for Algorithm 4.1's upper-bound formulation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Convex standard and adversarial training can attain lower objectives than the tested back-propagation recipes on a small binary CIFAR-10 subset.

record.peer_reviewed: SIAM Journal on Mathematics of Data Science
record.problems: The relevant CIFAR-10 results are binary-classification experiments on a 600-image downsampled subset. The reported training metrics are losses/objective values rather than training classification error; the text gives no matching error rates or classification-error threshold for them. The recipes and architectures therefore differ substantially from V1's stated setting.
record.rows_left_out: Validation accuracy, clean/adversarial accuracy, and the other reported accuracy results are not training classification error. Table 2 and Table 4 concern MNIST; the CIFAR-10 GPU result reports validation accuracy only. Figure 5 presents loss curves without a separately stated numeric result for training classification error.

untested.parts: Training classification error of sufficiently large convolutional networks on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, including corrupted labels, and the stated smaller-model, early-stopping and regularization qualifications.
Teacher-student ReLU problems and spurious-local-minimum frequencies as teacher width and student overparameterization vary.
Depth-dependent training degradation and prevention through identity shortcuts or the specified initialization alternatives.
Comparative effects of activation-matched, Gaussian and orthogonal initialization on training speed and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, transient loss increases, curvature evolution and subsequent recovery or divergence.
Training speed and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization, including Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: Table 5's objective assignments follow its row order and the accompanying comparisons; displaced objective entries caused several extraction errors. Appendix A.2 extends the convex formulation to batch-normalized networks but provides no with-versus-without normalization speed comparison. General statements about initialization sensitivity and vanishing gradients do not test V4.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, SGD or Adam from random initialization as specified, multiclass classification, or the effects of smaller models, early stopping and regularization on classification error.
